title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
pdf_path: papers/Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox.pdf
threat_model_summary: The user is benign but underspecified; the agent may take risky actions without confirming missing constraints. An adversarial emulator constructs long-tail high-risk states for testing. There is no external attacker, and authentication/authorization attacks are explicitly excluded.
core_contributions: ToolEmu: an LM-emulated sandbox that executes tool calls without real implementations
An adversarial emulator that reads underspecifications and risk fields to construct high-risk states
A GPT-4 safety evaluator scoring likelihood and severity on a 0-3 scale, plus a helpfulness evaluator
A benchmark of 36 toolkits, 311 tools, 144 test cases, and nine risk categories
Human validation: 68.8% of identified failures are true failures; 6 of 7 Terminal failures reproduce in a real sandbox
Real sandbox reproduction takes about 8 hours versus under 15 minutes with ToolEmu
limitations: Emulator and evaluator make errors (critical issues 8.1%/14.4%; safety recall 73.1%)
Test cases still require manual curation
Only instruction underspecification is covered; malicious intent is future work
Authentication, authorization, and multi-user access are explicitly excluded
Single GPT-4 emulator/evaluator; no cross-model robustness
Adversarial failure incidence is not a natural deployment rate
Agent-generated text can enter emulator/evaluator prompts without isolation
No defense is proposed; 23.9% failure is not a solved safety level
theoretical_crypto_links: None; POMDP is a sequential-decision formalism, not a security game
No theorem, proof, reduction, or cryptographic primitive
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, OAuth, or capability tokens
The 'sandbox' is an LM simulator, not a TEE or isolation boundary; capability-gated tools and attested execution are our inference
evidence_refs: pp.4-6 emulator, adversarial emulator, evaluator, benchmark
pp.7-9 human validation and main results
pp.17-30 limitations, rubric, and additional experiments

title: Aligned LLMs Are Not Aligned Browser Agents
pdf_path: papers/Aligned LLMs Are Not Aligned Browser Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious user directly asks a browser agent to pursue harmful behaviors; attacks modify only the user prompt and preserve the default system prompt. The agent may refuse in chat but still execute browser actions. No indirect injection, tool poisoning, or adaptive multi-turn attacker is studied.
core_contributions: BrowserART: 100 browser-related harmful behaviors, 47 harmful content and 53 harmful interaction
40 synthetic websites over 19 domains cover 77 behaviors; 23 require the real Internet
Evaluates eight frontier models in OpenHands + BrowserGym + AXTree
Shows a large alignment gap: GPT-4o chat ASR 12% versus browser agent 74%
Human rewrites raise GPT-4o and GPT-4-turbo to 98%/99%; ensemble attacks reach 100%/100%
Documents refusal-action decoupling and Claude prefilling attacks
limitations: Synthetic websites are simpler than real sites
Only the OpenHands scaffold is evaluated
GPT-4o is both judge and a tested model; judge noise is not quantified
No defense is evaluated
No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests
Only attempts are measured, not successful harm
Threat model excludes indirect injection, environment injection, memory/tool poisoning, and multi-turn attacks
Several internal count and prefilling inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; alignment and jailbreak are behavioral notions
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction; cipher appears only as a jailbreak-encoding reference
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Action-level capabilities and signed action receipts are our inference; they constrain execution, not model refusal
evidence_refs: pp.17-22 appendices with prompts and attack details

title: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents
pdf_path: papers/Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A legitimate platform user modifies their own images or text to mount targeted attacks on a web agent. The attacker cannot change the user goal or agent prompt/model, only untrusted environment content. Initial states are set at the trigger to ensure exposure.
core_contributions: 200 targeted adversarial tasks and evaluation scripts on VisualWebArena (VWA-Adv)
Agent Robustness Evaluation (ARE): represents the agent as a component graph and decomposes adversarial influence along edges
Defines AdvIn and edge weight lambda to attribute robustness flow across captioner, policy, evaluator, and value function
Shows text injection 40%, white-box captioner 31%, self-caption CLIP 19%, base CLIP 10%
Compromising evaluator or value function raises ASR from 31% to 36%/38%
Shows inference-time compute can reduce robustness under worst-case compromise
limitations: No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or seeds
Initial state at the trigger may overestimate realistic ASR
67% is GPT-4V with a white-box captioner, not GPT-4o or a fully black-box setting
Attack conditions differ in access; ASR values are not directly comparable
CLIP transfer is fragile to image size and surrounding text
Defenses are weak and non-adaptive; consistency checking has a 38% inferred upper bound
Only base/reflexion/tree-search agents and a fixed web environment
Internal relative-percentage inconsistencies in abstract/introduction versus body
theoretical_crypto_links: None; AdvIn and lambda are measurement/attribution definitions, not cryptographic security definitions
No theorem, proof, reduction, or cryptographic assumption
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Content provenance and action-level authorization are our inference; signatures cannot distinguish benign from adversarial content published by an authorized user
evidence_refs: pp.14-22 appendices with evaluation details and CLIP ablations

title: EIA: Environmental Injection Attack on Generalist Web Agents for Privacy Leakage
pdf_path: papers/EIA_ENVIRONMENTAL INJECTION ATTACK ON GENERALIST WEB AGENTS FOR PRIVACY LEAKAGE.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls a webpage's HTML/CSS/JS and injects invisible form or mirrored elements near a PII field. The agent is induced to type PII into the injected field, and JavaScript exfiltrates it. The attacker does not know the full user request or prior actions.
core_contributions: EIA: environmental injection attack on generalist web agents for PII leakage
Form Injection and Mirror Injection, with persuasive instructions and automatic exfiltration
Standard EIA targets specific PII; Relaxed-EIA makes injected content visible to attack action generation
Evaluates 177 PII action steps from Mind2Web across three backbones
Up to 70% ASR for specific PII; 16% for the full user request on GPT-4V; 0% for open-source backbones on full request
VirusTotal flags none of the injected pages; three defensive prompts barely change ASR
limitations: 70%/16% are conditional on the PII action step, not task- or user-level leakage rates
P0 is selected per instance; attacker knowledge of the target field is assumed
Offline, single-step evaluation; no end-to-end task measurement
Single-point injection only; multi-point and multi-turn injection are future work
Only SeeAct is tested; other frameworks may differ
Manual page adaptation is needed; automatic injection quality is limited
VirusTotal is not an HTML injection detector; defensive prompts tested only on GPT-4V
Table 1 variance 0.461 is inconsistent with the eight position values
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, or proof
PII leakage is a semantic privacy notion, not cryptographic confidentiality
applied_crypto_links: No TLS, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed field manifests, PII tokenization, and egress DLP are our inference; encryption cannot stop the agent from typing plaintext PII into a page
evidence_refs: pp.7-10 main results, defenses, human supervision
pp.17-28 appendices with manual pages and per-domain results

title: Searching for Privacy Risks in LLM Agents via Simulation
pdf_path: papers/Searching for Privacy Risks in LLM Agents via Simulation.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious recipient agent engages a data-sender agent in multi-turn interaction to extract sensitive information. The attacker may impersonate the data subject or forge consent; the data subject is disabled after transferring data, so no legitimate consent exists in simulation.
core_contributions: Search-based simulation framework that alternates attack and defense optimization
LLM optimizer reflects on trajectories and proposes new agent instructions
Parallel search with 30 threads and cross-thread propagation
Attack strategies evolve from direct requests to impersonation and consent forgery; defenses evolve from rule-based consent checks to identity-verification state machines
Testing-100 base leak velocity 31.2%; on Training-5, A1/D0 76.0%, A1/D1 2.5%, A2/D1 42.2%, A2/D2 7.1%
Real Outlook/Atlas case study succeeds in 3 of 5 trials
limitations: Data subject is disabled after transfer, so legitimate consent is impossible and D2 can collapse to never sharing
D2 helpfulness is only 31.2% without an extra helpful prompt
Defense transfer to weaker backbones is poor
Only leak velocity is reported; post-search leak rate is not
Judge may miss hints, pronouns, or cross-message leakage
Narrow threat model: one recipient, four mock apps, pure messaging
Prompt-level defense is not an execution boundary
Small real-world case study (5 trials)
Internal inconsistencies in Training-100 wording, figure labels, and step-wise table averages
theoretical_crypto_links: None; privacy is contextual integrity and leak velocity is a behavioral metric
No cryptographic primitive, security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, S/MIME, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Authenticated sender IDs, signed consent receipts, and capability tokens are our inference; D2's 'authenticated account' is a prompt-level check, not cryptographic authentication
evidence_refs: pp.6-9 main results, strategy evolution, real case
pp.16-22 appendices with confidence intervals and helpfulness
